blind_spots.blind_spot: The product is a targeting sensor, but nothing names where the track goes
blind_spots.operator_reality: A line of bearing or a geolocation from a Group 2 UAS only becomes a target when it lands in a C2 or fires system in a format that system accepts — CoT into TAK, VMF or Link-16 into the fires chain, or a specific ingest at the ground control station. 'ISR-T' claims the T. Across the whole site there is no mention of TAK/ATAK, CoT, Link-16, or any mission-system hand-off, which is the seam where an integrated payload stalls at the unit even after the airframe integration works.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: Their engineering identity is RF and DSP (UWB vector sensors, geolocation without GPS); the message-format and C2-integration layer belongs to whichever integrator bolts them on, so it has never been their deliverable — and consequently has no owner when a unit asks for it.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: ASI empowers you to know the unknown — detecting, and targeting RF threats from a single platform without mission crews or external coordination.

blind_spots.blind_spot: SIGINT/COMINT collection with no classified-handling or accreditation path described
blind_spots.operator_reality: COMINT and ELINT product is classified at the moment of collection. Getting it off the aircraft and to a user means a cross-domain path, an accredited ground segment, and cleared storage — plus company-level CMMC/NIST 800-171 and ITAR handling for the sensor's own performance parameters. None of that appears in ~1166 words. For a 15-person shop, a failed CMMC assessment or a missing cross-domain plan can stall a transition that the hardware has already earned.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: As a long-time SBIR performer they have delivered into government labs and integrators who already owned the classified enclave; the burden only becomes theirs when a unit wants the capability outside that arrangement.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: SNITCH delivers single-ball / single platform, precision RF 3D DF and targeting of much larger platforms on Small UAS. Supports COMINT, SIGINT, and ELINT modalities.

blind_spots.blind_spot: Three-week concept-to-flight is an integration demo, not a fieldable configuration
blind_spots.operator_reality: A payload flying on a contractor-owned Vanilla UAS in three weeks and the same payload flying on a unit's aircraft are separated by an airworthiness release for the modified configuration, an approved weight-and-balance and EMI/EMC case, GFE interface control on the host, and a training and spares plan for the crew that maintains it. That gap is measured in quarters, and it is where SBIR-funded hardware most often dies — the demo proved the physics and nobody funded the paperwork.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: Speed of integration is their best marketing asset and a genuine engineering achievement, so it gets published as the headline; the airworthiness and sustainment tail is invisible until a program office asks for the release.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Platform Aerospace and ASI Achieve Concept-to-Flight Integration of the SNITCH RF ISR-T Payload on Vanilla UAS in Under Three Weeks

opener_hook: ASI's sbir.gov profile shows 8 Phase II awards since 2010 against a 15-person company, and the SNITCH pages specify the payload down to 3.5 lbs and 40 W — but nowhere on asigint.com does an ISR-T product say where the track goes: no CoT, no TAK, no fires-cell hand-off named.
what_they_do: Builds ultrawideband passive RF direction-finding and geolocation payloads small enough for Group 2 UAS, giving single-platform SIGINT targeting without GPS or datalinks.
